claims.text: Nickel-based superalloy components have an inherent susceptibility to hot cracking and related defects in heat-affected zones produced by traditional fusion welding.
Localized friction stir processing can be used to repair or improve damaged surface areas of nickel-based superalloy components.
Friction stir processing uses a non-consumable tool.
Tool rotation near 800 rpm and traverse speed near 100 mm/min are optimized settings for this nickel-based-superalloy treatment.
Processing under ambient conditions limits FSP heat input.
Friction stir processing modifies material below its melting temperature.
Friction stir processing produces severe plastic deformation in the treated surface.
Friction stir processing dynamically recrystallizes the nickel-based-superalloy surface into a fine-grained layer.
Friction stir processing induces uniform compressive residual stresses in the treated layer.
Fine grains and compressive residual stresses delay the initiation and propagation of hot cracks.
The FSP-treated surface will have higher hardness.
The FSP-treated surface will have improved wear resistance.
The FSP-treated surface will have improved corrosion resistance.
FSP will delay surface-crack initiation under cyclic or aggressive service environments.
The hardness, wear, corrosion, and cracking performance of FSP-treated surfaces will exceed both fusion-welded repairs and untreated surfaces.
The intervention will perform effectively on nickel-based superalloys under aggressive operational conditions.
Complex component geometry can limit the uniformity of FSP treatment and require further process tuning.
Promising laboratory-scale results support the proposed benefits of the method.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis assumes FSP has been optimized for consistent treatment across complex geometries, whereas the conditions restrict it to relatively simple topologies and the boundary and uncertainty fields state that complex geometries still require optimization and may not be treated uniformly.
